speakeroldname: Hon. James Hugh Faulkner (Secretary of State):
subsubtopic: IMMIGRANT RESIDENTS TO BECOME CITIZENS AND TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL SUPPORT TO NATIONAL VOLUNTARY ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about a group of integrated programs which the government is undertaking to encourage eligible resident immigrants to obtain their citizenship and to provide financial support to national voluntary organizations engaged in stimulating a greater awareness among Canadians of the meaning and significance of citizenship.
Since the government does not oblige anyone to take out citizenship, there is no exact number of Canadian residents who now qualify. However, we estimate that there are over 850,000, possibly a million, immigrant residents in Canada who could now apply for citizenship.
As in other democracies, ours is not a coercive society. This is especially true of the registration of new citizens. The government can readily make available a range of services and essential information to them about these services. But it is up to the individual to initiate voluntarily the procedures leading to equal status with other Canadians. It will be a gentle invitation, this call to citizenship.
It is to extend the present registration and counselling facilities, and to add to the information at the disposal of potential citizens, that I am announcing today an additional budget of $2 million.
The Department of the Secretary of State has been receiving requests for the provision of special services for potential citizens. To help respond to the need, the services of citizenship branch officials and citizenship courts are being broadened in areas where the population density is high and the immigrant concentration is heavy.
New branch offices are being opened in Quebec City, in Brampton and Barrie, Ontario, and in Kelowna, British Columbia. On an experimental basis, travelling teams of citizenship registration officials will be located in "target areas" in Toronto, Montreal, Hamilton and Vancouver. They will be available upon demand to take applications and answer questions in such places as work sites, shopping centres, and recreation centres. There are plans for a storefront office in a busy location in Toronto, to make citizenship registration services as informal and as accessible as possible. The aim is to make the services available to people in the familiar surroundings of their own communities. Where we can, as with the storefront office, we also want the hours of service extended into evenings and weekends.
In support of this extension of court services, there will be a promotion program in the media, with emphasis on local newspapers. It is anticipated that there will also be some use of pamphlets and posters, and some reliance on radio and television.
A third program is the development of new resource materials to be provided to citizens and potential citizens to help them learn about Canada. These will include specially designed and specially written booklets, attractive and up to date, and audio-visual materials and kits for the use of individuals and citizens' groups.
It is with considerable pleasure that I announce today the first grants to be made under our new program of support to voluntary organizations engaged in special projects to reinforce the meaning and importance of our common citizenship. These grants will go to the Canada Studies Foundation in Toronto and the Canada Committee in Montreal.

Mr. Speaker, we of the Progressive Conservative party totally endorse the government initiative to assist those who come to this country to understand and to use their rights. We wish those who emigrate to Canada to do so with a genuine involvement.

At the same time, Mr. Speaker, we are aware, as are the ministers involved, of woeful shortcomings. There are no reliable figures available as to the number of illegal immigrants in this country. It is truly disgraceful that the honest must often wait for years, subjected to great anxiety through a cumbersome and outdated appeal process-

It is a disgrace that newcomers are given such hopelessly inadequate instruction in the new society into which they enter, and I hope that the government announcement today reflects a serious coming to grips with this problem.
Fully two-thirds of those who immigrate to this country are below the age of 30. We must keep this fact clearly in mind while developing immigrant services. Their access to the rich multicultural resources of Canada must be assured. Their full acceptance as Canadians should they desire to become citizens ought to be guaranteed. tion between native and naturalized citizens. This is surely in the spirit of the minister's initiative, and would certainly make citizenship more attractive to our resident immigrants.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me emphasize that the immigrant to this country has three major areas of difficulty: the first is one of information, often including a language barrier. The government has recognized its responsibility in general terms in this area, but we would like to see far more sensitivity shown with respect to the type and particular needs of immigrants for information, particularly for those who come from a radically different cultural background. The second great problem is loneliness. Here the direct role of the state is limited, yet that of its indirect influence is substantial. We must not allow the immigrant to disappear in our national debates on linguistic and cultural issues. Finally, there is a substantial economic problem. Many barriers are placed in the way of the newcomer; many of those with substantial skills are forced to work in positions and at wages which are far below their capacity, and all of Canada is made poorer by the limiting of their potential contribution.

The government has a positive role to play in those three areas. We have been delighted with the announcement of the minister, but I would like to express our wish that tjie government will integrate with efficiency and understanding those who come over to live in the Canadian community.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my party I welcome the statement made this afternoon by the minister as a first step in a broad, general review and extension of government services to immigrant people in Canada. The minister has given us a firm assurance in committee that such an overhaul of the programs being presented by his department is now under way and, taking him at his word, we look forward to further developments of a similar nature in future.
I have no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that the citizenship outreach program outlined this afternoon by the minister is not only needed but overdue and that it will prove to be well utilized so long as it operates on the principle that its prime concern is to meet the needs and convenience of its clientele and not those of the officials. The pilot experiments conducted in recent years by the department indicate that the present program, extended as it is, will be fully used. I would stress that the question of the hours of the services is crucial to the success of this program, and I would say to the minister that I hope the plan to operate it in the evenings and on weekends will not be limited merely to one storefront office but will include the mobile teams as well. I also hope that the department will establish advance liaison with the communities through existing organizations as well as the specialized media that often publish in the language of the immigrant community.
I would also point out that there is abroad a mystique to the effect that successful application for citizenship may involve answering tough questions or examinations. This

has in the past proved to be an inhibition to applications for citizenship. I hope that the promised programs to be undertaken by the department will assure that the process of applying for and receiving citizenship is an encouraging rather than a discouraging one.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, we look forward, as I said, to the continuing overhaul and extension of government programs aimed at new Canadians. I would emphasize that this process should be undertaken in close consultation with the communities affected as well as with provincial and municipal governments. I conclude by hoping that the program will extend beyond the range of the immediate services indicated in this afternoon's statement to the educational and cultural fields.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the
announcement just made by the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) in order to assist the voluntary groups dealing with immigrants is full of good intentions, and I believe that the whole House agrees with that decision.
However, it is necessary that those applying to emigrate to Canada be well informed. Rather unfortunate situations happened in the past, and I just have one in mind, Mr. Speaker. A Frenchman made an application to come over to Canada, and the Canadian immigration office in France told him that he absolutely had to speak English in order to emigrate to Canada and work here. With that information, the applicant went back home and managed to follow intensive courses in English, and after one year, he applied again at the immigration office. He was then accepted and once in Canada, in the province of Quebec, he went over to Normetal Mine, in my constituency, to take a job as a miner. Upon his arrival he realized that there were no English-speaking persons working in that industry. You can appreciate his disappointment in the face of that situation. He lost a year merely because of this anomaly.
In my opinion, steps should be taken first of all to properly advise those who want to become Canadian citizens. Then, the procedures for granting Canadians immigrants citizenship certificates should be instituted early enough for them to receive their papers when the time comes. Of course, cases may differ but, in my opinion, they should not be considered separately.
Some immigrants who want to qualify for Canadian citizenship could certainly meet our requirements within a year. However, there are others-a limited number, I am glad to say-who will never really become Canadian citizens. In all fairness to those who have been accepted among us, they should be granted their certificates of citizenship as soon as possible, when the time comes, so that they may become Canadian citizens.

June 6, 1973

Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time because today, June 6, marks the twenty-ninth anniversary of D-Day, and I am sure I speak for all members of the House and all Canadians in requesting a moment to pay homage to those valiant soldiers who took part in the allied invasion of Normandy.
Canadian veterans who took part will reflect today, I am sure, wherever they may be, on events which took place on the beaches of France some 29 years ago and think of their comrades who fell by their side and were denied the chance to return to Canada to avail themselves of the great opportunities of our growing and prosperous country. It is significant that today, 29 years later, the overriding topic that we are discussing across our nation is national unity and we are trying to attain this goal by legislation and with words. Yet we fail to recognize that we started to become a great nation because thousands of our young citizens from 1939 to 1945, including many who sit here as members of parliament, volunteered to fight for their country in far-off lands to defend Canada and the free world against the greed and lust for power of other nations. They fought together regardless of race, creed, colour or origin. They fought united as Canadians.
Hear, hear!

We can continue to build a greater nation if we take time to reflect and take an example from the comradeship which was instilled in our veterans through suffering together on the battlefield, a comradeship that will remain in their hearts as long as they live. We should think of this today. Let us ever remember the thousands of our veterans who lie in graves in foreign countries because of their duty to their country. Let us remember those veterans who returned, maimed and disabled, and who must look to us for help. Let us never forget our responsibility to those veterans who, by their sacrifice, protected our freedom to govern and to build a great nation for those of us who remain, a nation with pride, prosperity and peace, a nation with unity and comradeship among all Canadians.
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if they all run away they will obviously understand nothing.
We have just voted on one amendment. I do not think I am entitled to comment on this vote. However, what I find strange in the resolution of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is its lack of clarification. For instance, I went through the nine points submitted to Parliament. We have just decided that this resolution cannot become law but will still remain a resolution. Paragraph (6) reads as follows, and I quote:
(6) that unilingual incumbents of bilingual positions may elect to become bilingual and undertake language training, or transfer to another job having the same salary maximum, or, if they were to decline such a transfer, to remain in their positions even though the posts have been designated as bilingual;
I think that this completely destroys the resolution.
On television last night I heard the remarks of the member for Matane (Mr. De Bane). He was saying that this resolution will not in the least improve the situation.
Generally speaking, I agree. For the last few years we have been talking about official languages, bilingualism, equal treatment for French- and English-speaking Canadians and after three of four years of tentative action here and there we hear the Commissioner of Official Languages, Mr. Spicer, say that bilingualism has become a gross farce to the disadvantage of French-Canadians.
I do not intend to fight the assistance which the government wants to grant to our linguistic elements. However, I must quote a statement made by the former leader of the Progressive Conservative Party, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), as recorded on page 4396 of Hansard of June 4:
-He did not tell-
-meaning the Prime Minister-
-He did not tell the House why it is that at a time when critical

national issues confront us, parliament is being asked by the Prime Minister to masticate material already digested.
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. member used polite terms to say roughly what the Prime Minister said to the Lapalme boys a few years back.
The discussion of the past few days allows us to repeat what we have been saying for a number of years, that those are only pious wishes expressed in the House. In fact, even during this session we have seen how various departments make light of bilingualism or biculturalism and care little about treating English-speaking and French-speaking Canadians equally.
I have here a letter from the Department of Transport- the minister just left-addressed to:
Champlain Service Emilien Dube Riviere Portneuf Saguenay, Quebec
Mr. Dube does not know a word of English. But he is sent a document which reads as follows:
Transport Transports NEWS-NOUVELLES Canada Canada
It is entirely in English, two full pages, and not a word of French. The Department of Transport and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) sent that news letter to Riviere Portneuf in the Saguenay area to Mr. Dube who does not know a single word of English.

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext: It is a mistake!

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
It is a mistake? Then let us take another department, Mr. Speaker. I have here another letter, and I quote:
Plant Products Division Ottawa, Ontario K1A 0C5
May 29, 1973
Mr. Louis Paquin 77 Rue St. Thomas Montmagny, P.Q.
Mr. Paquin does not know a word of English. He received a letter signed by:
R. H. Davidson Feed Unit
It is certainly not "fed" neither in English nor in French.
Mr. Speaker, that is a letter written entirely in English from one of the divisions of the Department of Agriculture, and this occurred after three, four or five trial years.
Mr. Speaker, eleven years ago, when I was requesting from Air Canada more French spoken by its stewardesses, I used to receive the following reply: Yes, this is going to be improved.
When we were elected in 1962, the Parliamentary Rules were written in English and I must pay tribute to the former Prime Minister of Canada, the right hon. member for Prince Albert, who gave instructions to translate the Parliamentary Rules into French as early as 1962.

June 6, 1973

At present we travel by plane, for instance, between Montreal and Vancouver. It still happens that we cannot get a French answer on the plane. Mr. Speaker, I have nothing against a young lady-whether her name is Smith, Lanier, Caouette or Trudeau, I do not mind-but let them give us services in both languages! I would object if a stewardess could not speak English to English-speaking passengers. I am convinced that no English-speaking Canadians would tolerate unilingualism on Air Canada flights, over the CBC or in any other Crown Corporation.
Mr. Speaker, this is not asking too much but we have not yet succeeded in obtaining it and now the government is putting forward a resolution which says that any incumbent of an English unilingual position may elect to undertake French language training and keep his position if he wants to, even though he does not want to become bilingual. This is the whole matter which generates division throughout Canada.
We are spending millions of dollars to tell Englishspeaking Canadians to learn French, and French-speaking Canadians to learn English, although we will never succeed in making an English speaking individual out of a French Canadian nor a French speaking individual out of an English speaking one. This is a point that we must always keep in mind. We will never succeed in doing it.
But we must find a solution that seems acceptable to both groups, a solution allowing English-speaking and French-speaking Canadians to preserve their respective characteristics. I note that for the past three, four or five days the resolution has been criticized by all opposition leaders and by other members. At one point, the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) decided to move an amendment aimed at giving the force of law to a useless resolution. This is far from being very bright.
Mr. Speaker, we would like to move an amendment. My friend the member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) referred to it last Thursday and I would like to develop those points which we want to explain clearly in this House and outside for the benefit of all Canadians.
Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte):
That the motion be amended by removing, after "the foregoing:1* in the fourth paragraph, the nine principles which are listed, and substituting therefor the following:
(1)	Bilingualism cannot be considered as a basic factor of
qualification.
That is clear. If an English-speaking person is more qualified than a bilingual person in a certain field, he must be given the job even though he is unilingual. In doing so, we respect both the English- and French-speaking people in Canada. This would work both ways. We should not look for difficulties where there are none as we are doing right now.
A moment ago, I referred to airline stewardesses. Mr. Speaker, often times, a unilingual English stewardess gets a job with Air Canada. But a French Canadian stewardess who is not bilingual cannot get a job even in Montreal, even in Rouyn-Noranda, my hometown. Why should one have to speak two languages and the other be accepted though unilingual?
Official Languages
If we had truly parallel administrations for the whole nation we would not have the kind of situation we have at present. Then, as specified in our amendment, and I quote:
(1)	that bilingualism cannot be considered as an essential factor of competence;
(2)	that the knowledge of both official languages is required only for administrative positions where it becomes a criterion of competence, such as telephone operator, hostess, train conductor, receptionist, etc.;
In such cases, the knowledge of both languages may be required.
(3)	that everyone is free to speak the language of his or her choice in Canada;
I find it rather stupid to tell a civil servant: If you want to save your job, learn French. In fact, why should we tell a man of 50: Learn the other language or you might lose your job, you will be transferred or we will make changes which will upset everything. When someone is 50 years old, it is not the right time to tell him: Learn the second language that you must know.
I said it everywhere in Canada: If we want one day both languages to be known throughout Canada, let us start in the first grade to teach both official languages to our children and in less than five years, we will have people who speak French in British Columbia, in Nova Scotia, in Quebec and in Ontario.
Then, it might be done, but nobody should have to learn another language at 50, especially if we must spend hundreds of millions of dollars and tell people: Learn this language, we will help you. Then again, there are more Anglo-Saxons to help than French Canadians who speak French; so English people are given more opportunities to learn French and French people to learn English.
Mr. Speaker, I go on quoting our amendment:
(4)	that, account being taken of geographical and demograph-ical circumstances, everyone in Canada has the right to be served and administered in the official language of his or her choice;
(5)	that unilingualism cannot prevent a civil servant in the Canadian government from being eligible for senior positions; . . .
That means that all present public servants would keep their positions if we applied a really Canadian national policy.
I resume the quotation:
.. . therefore, the government undertakes to set up, organize and implement a parallel administration, one English-speaking, the other French-speaking, in all departments of the federal government;
It is being done at the present time in the CBC, for instance, where there is an English network and a French network. That was established by the government of that time.
We have Air Canada with an English section and a French section. We have a president of our own and the English section also has its own. Do we ever see the English or the French squabbling over senior positions in Air Canada?

speechtext: ... in the CBC.

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext: I said the CBC.

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
No, you said Air Canada.

June 6, 1973
Official Languages

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Maybe, but I meant the CBC, where there are two presidents.
Now, we are not asking for the appointment of two ministers, but for two deputy ministers, and parallel administrations in all the Federal government departments. Thus, each department would have two sections: one English and one French. The size of each would depend on the needs. They would not have the same number of employees, of course, as there are fewer French-speaking Canadians than English-speaking Canadians.
Coming back to the amendment, I quote:
... the size of these sections shall be proportional to the requirements of their respective administrative needs, which means that the departments shall not necessarily have the same number of employees;
(b) these departments shall be autonomous entities with equal responsibilities up to the deputy minister level.
It would not matter whether the minister be Frenchspeaking or English-speaking!
I continue the quotation:
.. . both the English-speaking and the French-speaking deputy ministers having similar authority and similar responsibilities;
Had we implemented that principle, we would not receive such letters in the Saguenay area, in Montmagny, or in areas of the province of Quebec where only French is spoken.
Mr. Speaker, paragraph (c) reads as follows: promotions in each department shall be based exclusively on merit.
Promotion should be granted to a civil servant not because he speaks French or English, but because of his actual skills.
Those are the points we would like this House to understand so we can finally stop quarrelling all across Canada and hearing the Anglo-Saxons say that French-speaking Canadians demand too much and French-speaking Canadians complain that English take everything.
Mr. Speaker, with parallel administrations, we would certainly have gained much ground. For instance, when you see that $29,000 are now being spent in trying to make someone bilingual with hardly any positive results, that $54,000 or $55,000 are being spent to allow someone to learn the other culture in Canada, you must agree that these things will never be accepted by Canadians as a whole.
Someone will probably ask me: What is it going to cost the government? It will cost national unity. And we will achieve national unity provided the identity of everyone is respected, provided equal opportunity is given every Canadian with a law that allows everyone to be himself.
Mr. Speaker, as to the resolution moved by the right hon. Prime Minister, I did not attend the cabinet meeting, but I was told by a member of the Liberal party that the whole story was fabricated, made up and presented to the government by the Public Service Alliance of Canada. Then, if everything is settled in advance, why do we discuss those questions here? If the civil servants are the ones who decide for the government, who say to the

government: We are in charge, and you are going to act in such and such a way, why then should a resolution be submitted to us?
In a debate as this one, Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, the whole resolution is defeated by the sixth principle and the last paragraph which reads as follows:
(ii) do further approve the taking of measures, after consultation with employee representatives, designed to produce a greater use of the French language at all levels in the public service, through increasing, where practical, the number of French language units, through further recruitment efforts by the Public Service Commission, through training programs offered in the French language and by developing proposals, in conjunction with the governments of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, to enhance the bilingual character of the national capital region, thus helping to realize the objective of achieving, within the merit principle, full participation in the public service by members of both the anglophone and the francophone communities.
This is again total confusion. In one paragraph the objective is to save national unity whereas in another paragraph it is attacked. A third paragraph states: You can remain what you are; if you are not satisfied, do something else.
We are presenting objectively our amendement to the House and we believe that parallel administrations would be no disappointment to anyone ans would be helpful to everyone. We would no longer hear an English civil servant say: Down with French civil servants and vice versa but Canadians would be on the same footing before the law and the same chances would be offered to all Canadians.
That is the amendment we are proposing and I hope the House will study it most carefully.

DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose we all have certain oratorical cliches. One of mine is that I usually begin participation in debate by saying it is a great pleasure to take part in the debate. I do not say that this time. Indeed, I enter this debate with a certain heaviness of heart because I have a feeling that the whole discussion is not likely to be helpful, although I will say, and say with sincerity, that there have been speeches of a very high order and among those I would list that of my leader, that of the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis) and that of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). However, there have been other utterances, and I regret to say some of them by the Prime Minister, in this House which have not indicated statesmanship and which have not been conducive to national unity.
I heard the Prime Minister when he spoke on the draft address and I also recall-I wish I did not-his malicious oratory when he spoke of certain people ending up as elevator operators. On this issue, there have been too many irritants and too many occasions when thoughtful silence would have been preferable to the smart utterance. I do not wish to denigrate a public servant and suggest that one utterance should characterize his whole performance, but I think Mr. Spicer's remarks about the Rhodesians might have been far better left unsaid. I heard him also on the radio last Sunday and I thought, when one woman phoned in and said that one of her children had learned French and the other had not, I had detected his approach of zeroing in on the one that had not, rather than of commending her in respect of the one that had. I have been in public life long enough to know it is much easier to catch the attention of the press and the public by the dramatic overstatement. Indeed, if he seeks publicity, the way of the moderate is hard.
While regretting the introduction of this measure at this time, and deploring the extremists on either side of the argument, I certainly plan to support this resolution and thereby renew my commitment to bilingualism, no matter how imperfect and sometimes hurtful has been its implementation so far. There is no immutable law, no certainty which declares that this Dominion shall endure. But it is my determination and my commitment that no intemperate remark of mine, no unwillingness to compromise, no unreadiness to understand others' views and aspirations will make even a tiny contribution to the weakening of the great experiment in nation building which began in my province, and indeed in my constituency in 1864.

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
If I did not make this clear commitment I think I would be unworthy to represent the cradle of Confederation.
The Prime Minister the other night expressed the view that the existence of two official languages was not primarily because of any historical founding rights. I am inclined to give more weight to history on this matter. The British North America Act, the product of compromise and conciliation of the men of Canada, Nova Scotia, New
Official Languages
Brunswick, Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island did establish a bilingual parliament. This matter was formally settled over a century ago. About that particular document and that particular provision the great Liberal historian Professor Lower, has said:
Similarly, the spirit of the Act, removed all distinction of status between French and English. The Act symbolized an agreement between the races to live and let live and gave a formula for the solution of the antagonisms that had brought the wheels of government to a stop. French speaking Canadians could only point to one or two specific clauses in hard legal support of their 'rights', but their claim would be that there were but 'the evidence of things unseen', the crystallization into law of understandings reached behind the scenes, of the compromises and mutual confidence which alone could have brought forth Confederation.
In Confederation, English and French, after a stormy courtship, took each other for better or worse, and whether the marriage had much prospect of being happy or not, it must, like other marriages create a reasonable degree of equality between the contracting parties.
I love to quote Professor Lower, who was one of the greatest teachers I ever had, and one of the greatest Liberals I ever ran across. The last time I saw him I gave him a little party in Charlottetown, and when he took leave of me he said: "I wish you well, Heath, even though you are a Conservative."
I mention the British North America Act because surely if the parliament of the country is to be bilingual, and to be established as bilingual, it is normal and natural to assume that the administrative bureaucracy through which parliament functions should reflect that bilingualism. Doubtless part of our anguish and frustration today stems from the fact that we are seeking to do in a decade what was essentially neglected for ten.
I listened carefully to the hon. member for Temis-camingue (Mr. Caouette). I always listen to him, Mr. Speaker. I honour him as a good federalist. He comes out with some strange ideas at times, and with some practical suggestions too. When he refers to the delay in making bilingualism a fact I am very much in sympathy with him. He mentioned Beauchesne. When I came to this House Beauchesne was available only in English, and God knows it is hard enough to understand even written in your own language. Here I mention that Dr. Beauchesne was not a Scottish Canadian. His book was printed in English from 1922 to 1959, and its publication in French was one of the fine things that did take place under the administration of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbak-er), that and simultaneous translation in this chamber. Until 1959, French speaking members had the right to speak, but not the technical right to be heard by those who did not know their language. And of course, it worked the other way also.
As has been noted in this debate previously, principally by the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark) who made a most excellent speech, the earlier emotional tensions and divisions in this country were more heavily weighted on the religious rather than the linguistic side. Even the great Sir Wilfrid Laurier could write as late as 1911:
It is becoming more and more manifest to me that it was not reciprocity that was turned down but a Catholic premier.

June 6, 1973
Of tidal Languages
Making allowance for the shock and pain which we are told is felt by all holders of high office on defeat, it is interesting that Laurier felt no repudiation of his ethnic background or linguistic category. Tension, then, was over religion.
But these strains did come very close, down through our history, to being a continuation of what Lord Durham described in 1837 as "two nations warring in the bosom of a single state." Deep cleavages such as those over separate schools, the autonomy bills of 1905, the ne tempere decree, and regulation 17 have been with this country down through the generations, and we are naive to think that the question of disunity is unique to our day and age. Indeed, since we became a country it has always been the test of statesmanship to resist and diminish the centrifugal forces which in Canada, in such a vast country, come into play far too easily. Confederation was not easily attained. We have always underestimated the eminence of the Macdonalds, Cartiers, Browns, McGees, Tuppers and others who were great nation builders. It was not easy for them to bring the country together. Nor is it easy to keep it together. Without goodwill, moderation, reasonableness and conciliation it will not hold together.
Reference has been made more than once to Sir John A. Macdonald, the founder of my party and, I think, the chief founder of the country. He had many virtues and some vices. But while he could be intemperate in some things he was ever temperate, wise and moderate on the issue of relations between the two major groups comprising the dominion. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) quoted Sir John the other night in direct reference to the language issue, when Macdonald said:
I have no accord with the desire expressed in some quarters that by any mode whatever there should be an attempt made to oppress the one language or to render it inferior to the other; I believe that it would be impossible if it were tried, and it would be foolish and wicked if it were possible.
Those are fine, wonderful words. Many years ago Sir John A. Macdonald wrote to a Montreal editor, and I am sure many hon. members are familiar with this quotation:
The trouble is that you British Canadians can never forget that you were once supreme, that John Baptiste was once your hewer of wood and drawer of water. You struggle for ascendency. If a lower Canadian Britisher desires to conquer he must stoop to conquer. He must make friends with the French without sacrificing the principles of his race or lineage. He must respect their nationality. Treat them as a nation and they will act as a free people generally do-generously. Treat them as a faction and they will become factious.
The phraseology is antique but the spirit, the sentiment is there. And of that particular passage again my old mentor, Professor Lower, wrote:
-wise words, the beginning and end of our Canadian puzzle but by few indeed taken to heart.
I give one final quote from Dr. Lower, who must love to be forming part of a Progressive Conservative member's speech! Here, I recall what he said about Macdonald:
-his stand with respect to the race question was consistent throughout his life whatever the cost to himself ... he refused to raise the race cry at a time when he was in low political water.
I am proud that the father of my party in this, the eighty-second anniversay of his death, left such noble sentiments to guide us on this very serious matter. In
these difficult days it is our task, indeed our duty, to ameliorate not exacerbate those things which might divide us, moderate not accentuate the irritants which could weaken the frail fabric of federation, and at times indeed it appears frail. It is my belief that we would be unworthy of our present and our past if we brought to an end the experiment launched with wisdom and foresight by our political ancestors in Charlottetown in 1864. I intend to do my humble bit to help strengthen the dynamic unity of this country.
The hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) on Monday praised the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). I appreciate and I echo his sentiments. There is a deal of personalizing entering into this debate. Mr. Speaker, I attended my first political meeting at the age of 11, and I have had the privilege of knowing the greats and the near greats of my party over a good many years. I remember all the numerous defeats and the few victories, and it is an honour to know those who are dedicated to a political party because I believe that Lord Bryce is right, that parliamentary democracy cannot function without political parties.
I have never been reluctant to parade my belief in political parties, and in their function. I would like to say I rejoice in the mind and in the manner of the man who is now our leader. Him I have known for 25 years. I was extremely young when I first met him! He came to the leadership of our party pledged to do his utmost for the unity of Canada. He has adhered to that pledge, and no man of all the men who have led our party with honour and distinction, and I am not reluctant to praise them all, no man has been more honourable, more consistent, more faithful in his determination to place country ahead of party, and the unity of the nation ahead of any seeming temporary partisan or political advantage.

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
One of the great statesmen of an earlier age said that the worst ill which could befall any country would be for it to be divided on political lines paralleling lines of race or lines of religion. He said that that kind of strain no political entity could stand. To those who look only superficially, we might appear to be close to that situation in Canada today, but I say that those who look more deeply than that, know in fact that that is not the case.
One of the things of which I was most proud in the Leader of the Opposition-and I know he will not care for these references I am making-was that after the election on October 30, when it would have been natural and normal that he might have been disappointed in the response to his program and of his people in the province of Quebec, he wasted no time in recriminating, no time in repining, no time in regretting but said straightforwardly, simply and sincerely, "I would not feel content about forming a government with little representation from Quebec". This was a speech that he made in Edmonton, after that near miss on October 30. It is my belief that he will be forming a government and that he will be having representation from Quebec.

June 6, 1973

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Indeed, the more I see at close hand our new member from Quebec, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) I say that our setback there was only numerical and it is only temporary. Him, I honour as a man who serves his province, who serves his country with dignity, with presence, with moderation and with wisdom and I would class him, although he may not enjoy this sort of adulation either, as the modern Cartier of this nation. I think when this matter is disposed of and we move on to pressing things of an economic nature, that it is for all of us to set aside our differences, to ameliorate dissention and to make sure that in the development of the concept of bilingualism people are not injured. This, of course, is the great problem, when you take a good idea and apply it people are injured. This has been the problem that has caused anxiety to many, many Canadians.
I listened with interest to the hon. member for Temis-camingue (Mr. Caouette). I cannot say his resolution commends itself to me or to my colleagues. It seems to me that to follow the course which he has mapped out, to support the resolution which he has advanced would, for a long time to come, give firmness and fabric to the very thing we do not want in this country, that is the continuation of the two solitudes, an expression that a distinguished Mari-timer and great author used some years ago. I think we should be standing together and we should be governing the country together.
Not all of us will speak the same tongue. I notice that most people in this debate have expressed some of their remarks in English and some in French. I am not so confident of national unity that I would attempt to speak in French! I commend the present Leader of the Opposition who has become bilingual, and I commend members in the Social Credit Party for what they have done in this regard. But, as for their resolution, we do not want to preserve, to jell, the separation of our groups. We want to find ways where meaningfully we can work together to make the country the land of all, regardless of background. This surely was the vision of those who met in Charlottetown and Quebec City; this is what it was about.
I never liked to hear this expression "the patriation of the constitution"; I maintain the expression is "repatriation" because the constitution was made in Canada by Canadians, by people of the dominion and it was only a technicality that caused it to be processed in Britain. It was our achievement, by our great men of the nation, of the dominion. At times like this we have to be on the alert for those things which would divide that unity, which would diminish that entity, which was created by our political forefathers, men of wisdom, men of reason, men of understanding, men of broad vision. We must keep these visions of tolerance and understanding. These are the keynotes, these are what are called for in difficult days. In its application, bilingualism is difficult. People will be inconvenienced and worse, but we must set our eyes upon a high and noble goal and we must work together for it.
The hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark) was wondering about the motives of this resolution. I profoundly hope that no one introduced this measure as a device to diminish the effectiveness of my political party.
Official Languages
I profoundly hope that this is not the case but I am in a position to say-and I am not a stripling in the party any more-that any one who had that illusion was totally wrong. Our party is not a newcomer when it comes to concern for national unity. Down through the ages we have held beliefs and initiated practices that put us in the position where we have to take a back seat to no other group. Not that I am boasting that we are better than others or that we have more regard, but we have not been unmindful of those things which unite rather than divide the country.
In conclusion, I am happy to say that we are led by a man, the present Leader of the Opposition, who, while he may be short on charisma is long on character and who will give that kind of leadership in his present role as well as a role which will come his way before long I think, that will cause Canadians of all backgrounds and different languages to be confident that he is a fit and proper repository of their confidence, a man who has the statesmanlike qualities which marked men like Macdonald and Laurier, men of moderation and goodwill who have generally been the people in whom the Canadian people have reposed their confidence for the longest periods.
So, Mr. Speaker, while I have noted and deplored some of the irritating features of this matter, I renew my commitment to the principle of bilingualism. May it be a hopeful factor for building a better Canada; may it be a factor causing all Canadians to feel that this indeed is a land worthy of their confidence, worthy of continuing fidelity. I hope we will not soon again have to be asked to renew our belief in something which most of us made clear only a few years ago. Let us say that now the issue has been settled, let us make bilingualism work with fairness with justice, with efficiency for all.

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleagues tell me they are all behind me, and I shall feel secure-until I turn round. Being the whip of my party, I have sometimes tried to convince members not to take part in a debate in order to allow quick passage of a bill or resolution. However, in this debate I understand their feelings when they say they wish to speak. Having listened to the debate on this resolution, I feel that there is room and need for some of us who represent western prairie areas to express our feelings and opinions, in view of some of the remarks which have been made in this House.
I want to make my position perfectly clear. I do and will support the Official Languages Act. I do and will support the resolution presently before the House, even, I might add, if my party were of a contrary opinion to the one it presently holds, and they are not of that contrary opinion. Some speakers in this chamber have questioned our sincerity in debating this measure at this time. There is no greater question that this one relating to the unity of our country and its future. Any matter relating to that, whether it be the resolution concerning employment in the public service or the Official Languages Act, ought, without doubt, to be debated in this House when necessary.
4508

June 6, 1973
Official Languages
There are in this House fellow westerners whose opinions I have respected over the years. Included among them is the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker). I have always admired and respected him in his pursuit of his political career. Let me point out to them why it is necessary to debate this kind of resolution. In the past, authority has been exercised in such a manner that the relevance of this House has been brought into question by members, particularly by the right hon. member for Prince Albert, who has complained about the erosion of the powers of parliament. Therefore, I am pleased to see this resolution openly and freely debated in the House. I believe it is a resolution of importance and significance. I know of no place other than parliament where this question can be so effectively debated. Certainly, in this House we consider questions relating to national unity and questions of an economic nature. For a long time my party has espoused or proposed certain changes in our economic system in an attempt to solve those problems that divide our country on economic grounds. I will continue speaking on that subject as well, as I am sure the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) is well aware.
The hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) made an excellent speech today and enunciated the position that ought to be taken by members of parliament of this country and by the people of Canada generally. On our national coat-of-arms, if one cares to call it that, one will see a slogan that, translated, reads "From sea unto sea". Sometimes, in listening to debates in the House, in listening to my constituents and to people from all across Canada, I have felt that one word ought to be added to that motto-toleration. Our motto ought to read, "Toleration from sea unto sea". This nation cannot continue to exist if the two founding races, and the other races which have come to this country,-I use those words in a proper way-cannot learn to work together and function in an atmosphere of toleration. I believe that if one is a student, as I am, of Canadian history, one will find that this nation is unique. That cannot be denied.
I fear for its economic future because of foreign control and ownership of our resources. But Canada has maintained its identity as an independent nation of North America by reason of the operation of certain social and cultural forces. There are varied elements in our population. They are different. I believe that the difference of our cultural development, the difference of outlook, the difference in our social input, if you like, is to be attributed to the influence of the French fact, if one cares to call it that, in Canada. The fact that 7 million people living in one province use a language different from that in common use in North America, the fact that in areas like Saskatchewan there are thousands of French Canadians who are still adept at expressing themselves in French and in English, has, above all else in this country, helped us to maintain ourselves as an independent nation, as a nation together, instead of as a nation swallowed up by the United States of America. I have been talking about cultural matters and not economic matters. The cultural aspect of our country is, as I said, tremendously important in keeping this country together.
This resolution before the House, which I support, clarifies some aspects of bilingualism, as that relates to the

public service. In this connection I wish to read an article written by Mr. Carson. The headline is "Bilingualism in the public service". I shall read this to show why I hold the view I do. It reads in part:
We have undertaken, and will continue to undertake, programs aimed at attracting an increased number of French-speaking Canadians into the public service. We are very mindful of the fact that in the past, French-speaking Canadians have not had an even break when it came to being considered for a job in the public service. The current population of the service in the key occupations-the executive, scientific and profession, administration and foreign service, and technical categories-is 67,661. Of that total, 55,324 or 81.8 per cent are English-speaking and 12,337 or 18.2 per cent are French-speaking.
Given that the population breakdown in the country at large is about 28 per cent French-speaking to 72 per cent English-speaking, I would venture to say that much remains to be done before we can truly say that the public service is representative of the two main linguistic groups in Canada .. .
The overwhelming and traditional anglophone influence in the public service generates enough pressure to actually work against equal opportunity for French-speaking Canadians competing for jobs in the public service. Special recruitment programs help to counteract such pressure. During 1971, for example, 589 university students were recruited under the regular program, 449 of whom were English-speaking and 140 of whom spoke French as their mother tongue but were sufficiently bilingual to work in English, as we have traditionally required. One can see that our regular recruitment programs are not enough to attract and engage a sufficient number of French-speaking Canadians to offset this influence. With the addition of a special recruitment program, the French-speaking university recruitment total was raised to 398- not enough to redress the balance, but a step in the right direction.
The figures used show why the Parliament of Canada needs to deal with the problem respecting bilingualism in the Public Service. I believe that many problems were created because of the manner in which the government tried to implement its program in this regard in the last three or four years. Now, because of the result of the October 30 election, and because this is a minority parliament, the government has asked this House to express itself on a resolution, in an attempt to straighten out or accommodate the situation within the public service. I believe the resolution should be given full support. I commend the leader of my party for his position, other members of my party and other members of the House as well, who, as I do, support the resolution.
If we are to examine the future of this country, we have to recognize that this federal system has reached the position where in the next decade or so it must truly accommodate the fact that this is a bilingual nation, the fact there are two founding races, English and French. There must be tolerance to allow resolutions such as this to be discussed in parliament and by the public in a sound and rational manner in order to allow a continuing growth, not a tearing apart of this dominion of Canada.
I wish to deal with one aspect of this question which may interest members who participate in this debate. Some members have mentioned that unilingual French Canadians have difficulty getting jobs in the Public Service of Canada. I notice that most grievances filed under the Official Languages Act have been from unilingual Canadians of French background. Some hon. members, including a colleague on this side of the House, spoke of English Canadians who have become very angry because a
June 6, 1973

position has been designated as bilingual. They thought the program was all wrong. Therefore, there are these two forces creating tension.
In western Canada there are large settlements of French Canadians whose ancestors were pioneers. For example, in my constituency there are 4,000 to 6,000 individuals whose mother tongue is French. Some of the leaders in their society have a different view toward the Official Languages Act. Originally, they did not think it was very effective. They thought it was merely an attempt to get Quebec to feel part of this nation. Even though the area in which they live has been designated as a bilingual district, they thought the Language Act was a sop to Quebec and they were being left out of the picture. These people have struggled to maintain their group, as have many other groups in the province of Saskatchewan. These people have the only bilingual school that I am aware of in the province of Saskatchewan. They have had to fight constantly in terms of dollars and cents to keep that college in operation. I have never been more proud of a situation than when I attended the graduation ceremonies at College Mathieu three weeks ago. That is an example of a bilingual school teaching the two official languages of this country. Students were able to make their addresses and replies to different toasts and so on in the two official languages. That is an example of the kind of development there ought to be in Canada in terms of the use of another language by both major groups.
I realize that the party across the way has moved an amendment. I will cease my discussion on this matter as I am sure they wish to have more members participate. I will end on this note. The most important aspect of this question is for those of us who believe in tolerance and accommodation to accept that moral obligation. We must express that toleration and accommodation by supporting the principles and the carrying out of the Official Languages Act in a just and judicial manner. We must listen, conciliate and, at times, compromise. We must ensure that that accommodation and tolerance operate to maintain national unity in this country of Canada, which all of us want to see continue to exist.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the beginning of the debate on the motion introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), with a view to reopening a meaningless debate on bilingualism, I dreaded with some bitterness taking part in it because it seemed abnormal to me that in 1973, after a federal election, we should have to come back to the question of bilingualism in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the main motion which gave rise to this debate and prompted our leader, the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette), to move his motion a moment ago, is in my opinion-especially after listening to several speakers in this House-a device used by the great political parties, among others, to save face. That seems to me to be the purport of all the speeches I have heard.
I remember that after the election of October 30, 1972, in which the government had lost an almost unprecedented majority, the right hon. Prime Minister accused the Progressive Conservatives of having made contradictory
Official Languages
statements during the election campaign on the Canadian language problem; he said that at that time threats had been made on both sides and that in the Speech from the Throne, he would propose a resolution on bilingualism to settle this matter.
Now, this resolution was tabled in April and it is under study. The more I read it, Mr. Speaker, the more I find it unacceptable, hard to understand and to support. In fact, this motion does not change anything at all.
We must understand that a law called "Official Languages Act" has already been before Parliament. We must also understand that all the departments, since 1968, are governed by the bilingual policy generally based on the requirements of the Official Languages Act which was adopted by this Parliament and which recognizes an equal status to the two languages in the Civil Service and in Canada.
The departments are also guided by the Public Service Employment Act, the Translation Bureau Act and by the policy and directives set up by government.
But, before continuing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that the position of the Commissioner of Official Languages was created, as well as inquiry commissions. There was the Coulombe inquiry, within the Treasury Board. There was the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism that spent millions of dollars to learn what language people were speaking in Canada. It was discovered that in some regions of the country, people spoke English and that in others, they spoke French.
Since then, one concept is replaced by another: the concept of two nations, the concept of one nation, Francophones versus Anglophones, and we say: The others are to blame.
Within the various departments, within the Public Service, official statistics readily prove that not only is there no progress being made, but that several departments are moving backwards.
I know that many government members or others will say: That is not true. Then I will refer them to Hansard for Wednesday, May 16, 1973. As a result of such findings, our party has been prompted for a number of years to move a positive motion, and we will support it all the way.
Let us take the case of the National Defence Department. The minister will rise in the House and stand up for his department saying that bilingualism there is a fantastic achievement and that they spend thousands of dollars for that purpose. Let us read question No. 482 put on order paper by the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin) regarding the National Defence Department, and I quote:
2. What number and total percentage of that department's employees are (a) English unilingual (b) French unilingual (c) bilingual?
Here is the answer:
2. On 31 December, 1972, there were (a) 61,960 (76%) unilingual Anglophones (b) 10,422 (13%) unilingual Francophones ...
Let us consider, for instance, the Manpower and Immigration Department and the significance of our motion will be obvious. Some day we will have to bow to facts.
4510

June 6, 1973
Official Languages
I go on quoting:
2. What number and total percentage of that department's employees are (a) English unilingual (b) French unilingual (c) bilingual?
Now, regarding the Department of Manpower and Immigration, despite the Official Languages Act, promises and pious wishes from this and preceding governments, are we to believe that this department does not have such information? It does not know how many of its employees are unilingual English, unilingual French and bilingual. It does not know and I would be curious to hear the minister (Mr. Andras) tell us what he thinks about the bilingualism possibilities, progress of bilingualism and respect for both languages in his department.
The reply is this and I quote:
The information is not available from departmental records.
Yet, in the very same department, $111,000 were invested in 1970-71 for bilingualism, but bilingualism for whom, Mr. Speaker, if no one has not even any information available, if it is not even known who has been following these courses? What was the classification of the employees who took this course?
Do you realize that this department which spent $174,000 to develop bilingualism during fiscal year 1971-72, and which will spend $671,000 during fiscal year 1972-73, does not even know how many of its employees speak only French or English, and how many are bilingual?
To speak plainly, this is a policy worthy of an ostrich. This motion which has been presented to divert people and continue to divide Canadians, will solve nothing. On the contrary. The civil servant whose rights have been encroached upon and who tries to avail himself of this motion will eventually realize that, because it is only a declaration of principles, this motion has no legal value in court.
Mr. Speaker, for the Department of Manpower and Immigration to spend $671,000 on bilingualism without actually knowing the number of civil servants taking these courses is a disgrace.
Let us take for instance the Department of Labour. Maybe we shall finally find a department that works? Same question: Unilingual English-speaking employees:
2. a) 482, 71.4 per cent;
Unilingual French-speaking employees:
b) 1;
This means that bilingualism applied at the expense of French-Canadians through those courses, and this is unilateral. As the hon. member for Temiscamingue stated earlier, the opportunities for becoming bilingual are much greater-at any rate they are disproportionate-for the English-speaking civil servants than for the Frenchspeaking employees.
I could keep on quoting those statistics, but anyone can read. I will conclude with the Department of National Health and Welfare which is not only unable to say how many of its employees are unilingual English-speaking, unilingual French-speaking or bilingual but the answer is, as recorded on page 3821 of Hansard of May 16, and I quote:

2 and 3. Employees may only be considered as officially bilingual on the basis of having successfully completed the Public Service Commission second language proficiency test and met all standards set for their particular work category. Since this test is not compulsory, there may be certain persons who are in fact bilingual and who are not counted as such. However for the purpose of this question, all employees not bilingual, are considered to be unilingual.
These civil servants have certainly had a bright idea when they concocted this answer. And again I quote:
.. . There is at present, no basis for officially identifying unilingual French or unilingual English employees. The information requested in paragraphs 2 and 3 were not available before 1971. Listed below are the data . . .
This is the dead-end you reach with this bilingual policy advocated by the right hon. Prime Minister who is trying to turn French-speaking people into English-speaking people and vice versa whereas it would be so simple to leave everyone as they are and at a much lesser cost.
Mr. Speaker, an article published in Le Devoir of October 19, 1972 read as follows:
The federal government's program for the teaching of a second language has been an almost complete failure during the 1966-71 period.
Regardless of the method used to assess the results, it is obvious that the program was highly ineffective and awfully expensive.
This is borne out by a report. . .

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext: Give your references.

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I am quoting from Le Devoir of October 19, 1972.
I go on reading:
... a report of 300 pages completed in April 1972 by Mr. Andre Beaudet for the Treasury Board's task force on bilingualism.
"The Language Bureau's operation costs for those five years actually reached a sum of $54 million . . .
-namely $29,000 for each public servant. And for other public servants known as "senior officials" because they run the government, it cost $55,000 for each to become sensitized to the other culture in Toronto. Mr. Speaker, this clearly leads us nowhere.
The purpose of our motion is this: Instead of trying to make an Anglophone out of a Francophone and vice versa, we want Anglophones and Francophones to be at their place in the Public Service, without prejudice to the career or promotion of either because of their language.
It is ridiculous to base competence on the bilingual factor, Mr. Speaker. Competence should be based instead on the knowledge of the individual and his superior or average ability, but not on bilingualism.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to clarify a point of our policy. Yesterday I was discussing this motion with my Liberal colleagues who said: "Parallel services do not make any sense." Mr. Speaker, to answer those who are over-critical it is obvious that a policy of parallel services is difficult to implement, for example, in the Department of External Affairs. When we are dealing with the Chinese, we surely speak their language. Money knows no language, Mr. Speaker. If our department is dealing with the Secretary of State for External Affairs, it is surely with the department and not with a branch. We are referring to all the
June 6, 1973

federal departments or Crown corporations dealing with the public. We want those departments to be separate, one French-speaking and the other English-speaking. It does not harm anyone and we would be upholding the rights of everyone.
When I hear in the House speeches on national unity, on this magnificient and vast country, Canada, on the importance of speaking the two languages, of course I agree, Mr. Speaker. As the hon. member for Temiscamingue stated, we should do so in the early school years, we should give language training in the two languages in the schools, and the federal government could surely play an important role in the financing of this training. But we realize now that when a member of parliament or any citizen has any business to conduct with any department, and obtains a reply in English, that, Mr. Speaker, becomes unacceptable, when we know the costs of bilingualism.
What will it cost to remain oneself? When Frenchspeaking people communicate with the Department of Veterans Affairs, once our motion is agreed to, it is absolutely sure that they will be served in their own language by this department and that they can deal in French at all levels, even if they speak to the deputy-minister.
What will that cost, Mr. Speaker? No more than the present system, under which we flounder and have to work out percentages to know if there is progress or recession, while national unity wavers.
Mr. Speaker, I had a very unfortunate experience a month and a half ago when I went before the Canadian Transport Commission to stand up for some of our students. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) is going to say that he is not responsible for the Commission. But sooner or later someone will have to say he is responsible for something as far as the Commission is concerned.
I was unable to meet with anyone at the Canadian Transport Commission who spoke my language. I had to come back to my office and find someone who was bilingual on our floor. This person is fluent in both languages, better than I am. I should like to master both languages but it is a matter of time and I want to keep my own identity. In any case, I went back to the Canadian Transport Commission with this translator. The Commission could not even provide an interpreter. I was ashamed because I was accompanied by ten students and none could speak English, because they had all grown-up in a French-speaking community. And yet these young people were penalized because they spoke French, in the same way as a unilingual Francophone who would like to apply for employment with the civil service.
The fact that the applicant can speak both languages will be used as a proficiency criterion and he will be required to speak English adequately, otherwise preference will be given to a unilingual Anglophone or to a bilingual whose mother tongue is English.
Mr. Speaker, as long as we stand such a discrimination, as long as we are satisfied with pious wishes, as long as we play politics at the expense of French Canadians, we will contribute to dividing the country.
I heard Progressive Conservative members say that the Prime Minister's motion was meaningless and then they introduced a motion suggesting that this meaningless
Official Languages
measure be written into law. Mr. Speaker, this is their kind of logic.
The Liberals who find it funny are no better. They present a motion which, they say, will solve all problems, but about which the Progressive Conservatives say: If it is that good, write it into law, and then they are against it because they do not want it to become law.
For five days now we have been wasting our time. Pretentious speeches have been made but it remains that discrimination still exists within departments and Crown corporations. The fact is that if some progress has been made in the House with regard to bilingualism, it is because some men have stood up; as long as men, in this government or in the following ones, do not really stand up-it is not a matter of taking anything away from people but of seeing to it that these linguistic rights are truly respected-we will get nowhere.
This is why we are advocating the respect of cultural entities in Canada, the respect of languages and of every citizen within the Civil service. We are advocating a policy whereby, at any time of the night or day, any Canadian citizen, from the Pacific to the Atlantic, can communicate with his government, with a department-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. minister for his information, but if he knows his department so well, we will be able to speak of it to him.
To question No. 473 published in the Hansard, which reads in part as follows;
What number and total percentage of that department's employees are (a) English unilingual (b) French unilingual (c) bilingual?
The following answer was given:
(a) English unilingual, 12,360, 80 per cent; (b) French unilingual, 1,558, 12 per cent.
To the fourth part of the question which reads in part as follows:
. . . what was the total budget allocated for the development of bilingualism in that department?
The answer is, and I quote:
4. Total budget allocated for development of bilingualism is available only for the following years: 1969-70, $92,280; 1970-71, $59,100; 1971-72, $324,754; 1972-73, $976,900.

June 6, 1973
Official Languages
Surely that time, I went to the Canadian Transport Commission, and I was not lucky, Mr. Speaker, for I would have liked to see at least the result of an investment of almost $1 million for bilingualism, which I was not able to do. It would have been much easier for the Canadian Transport Commission to have a French-speaking section so that there would not have been any kind of problem.
Mr. Speaker, this seems extremely important to me. A lot of things might be said about this motion, but let us think seriously about it.
In an article by Claude Ryan in the paper Le Devoir, on June 1, 1973-it is sometimes a good thing to draw inspiration from people who observe the situation from outside and some people might be surprised to hear that members of the Social Credit Party read Le Devoir-one can read about the present policy of the government, and I quote:
this policy, when considered without any partisanship, represents a strategic withdrawal more than anything else . ..
Not only does the government reserve for itself the exclusive use of a capital document which belongs to all hon. members, but it asks the House to vote on the future of bilingualism without stating itself its own approach to concrete problems which exist in this area . . .
As long as this reality will not be more clearly admitted, we will likely waste-as has been the case for seven years-millions of dollars in programs of linguistic dusting which will always have restricted results . ..
Mr. Speaker, since they came to this House the Credit-ists have fought for the respect of French. When you consider that during one hundred years the Standing Orders in this House were in English only, that is a real shame. And I am ashamed of those Quebec members who represented us here and never dared to stand up and demand a translation.
Mr. Speaker, it is not out of bitterness that we demand equal rights for both languages. It is strictly because it seems abnormal to us to have to fight for the respect of a language. It seems to be a natural and legitimate right and we should not be fighting for something so essential, so vital and so human.
All Canadian citizens have the right to be served in their mother tongue. All Canadian citizens under the Canadian Bill of Rights are equal before the law, but they are not treated equally-in spite of the fact that the bilingualism policy is costing millions of dollars-when they approach departments or Crown corporations.
How many more years will we have to wait before we realize that the bilingualism policy will always have to be brought up again, that it does not really serve the interests of both languages? The cost of making a public servant who is 35 or 40 bilingual is $29,000, and even then the results are patchy, some are often so hard-headed that it cannot be done. Mr. Speaker, even if we spend $55,000 to teach the other culture to a public servant, when that public servant reaches 50, he will not be able to transmit his knowledge to his replacement. We will have to start all over again.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I am surprised to see that when public servants are hired now, they are judged according to their linguistic knowledge, and preference is given to those who are bilingual, so that French-speaking unilinguals-the majority in Quebec-hardly has a chance

to get a job in those departments, so that we will always go around in circles and continue to divide Canadians among themselves.
Mr. Speaker, the motion we introduced today is a valid one: it is positive and also suggests a solution to that problem.
We do not want to take anything from the Englishspeaking Canadians but we would like them to recognize the same rights to French-speaking Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, it is only at that cost that every Canadian citizen will really feel at home in his country. When I am in Toronto I expect to have to speak English. When a Torontonian comes to Victoriaville, my home town, he expects to have to speak French, but when the Torontonian or someone from Victoriaville calls upon a department they expect to be served in their mother tongue. And, Mr. Speaker, the easiest way to satisfy that legitimate right of those two Canadians who are equal before the law would be to give the French-speaking Canadian unit and the English one an English unit, so that both would be treated on an equal basis.
Before I resume my seat, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say I am eager to see this Parliament put an end to its division over matters of languages when such matters are already established facts-and that we discuss serious problems.
Bilingualism, Mr. Speaker, is obviously a serious and very important problem. This is why we are moving a positive and constructive motion to solve this problem. But, we will not do it by speaking for days and days about languages, by moving motions that mean absolutely nothing and have no value legally.
I would like the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Mar-chand) to indicate to me what would be the use of such a motion. Let us suppose that there is an obvious injustice within a department, that an appeal is lodged as provided for in the Public Service Commission Act and that this civil servant wants to protect himself, will he be able to use that motion to defend himself? No, and the hon. minister must admit it. This is true, as the game we are playing here settles absolutely nothing. It is nothing more than small vengeance by the right hon. Prime Minister against Higher Canada and, Mr. Speaker, that does not mean anything.
In any event, I sincerely hope that all my colleagues in the House will read this motion, consider it in depth and pass judgment on its merits. If we do it in a non partisan objective manner, I believe, Mr. Speaker that all Canadians will derive something positive from this debate. It would have been useful for once, to speak about languages, because we would then have had the assurance that every Canadian will be served in his own language, without depriving anybody of anything, but in respecting the equal rights of everyone.
