speechtext:
I realize I am allowed 40 minutes, Mr. Speaker, but if I take that long I will be speaking from now until the vote is called, thereby being the last member to speak on this subject, and I would not like to be in that position. As a member who voted against second reading of the Official Languages Act, may I say I have no reason to regret that vote. I am only sorry that my fears concerning that legislation are being realized. The proof of that fact is that we are now engaged in this debate, less than four years after the proclamation of that legislation.
Speaking as a representative from western Canada, I would say there is no objection to, or resentment of, those persons of French origin in this country. In point of fact, western Canada was settled by people from every part of the world. We have learned to live with and judge one another for what we are, and by that I mean what we can do, what the value of our word is and the interest we take in our communities and neighbourhoods.
The fundamental fear of the bilingual program as administered by this government is simple; it is that the public service at the senior or executive level will be completely dominated by people, whether they be anglophone or francophone, from the Ottawa Valley, Quebec and northern New Brunswick. It has long been the belief in western Canada, and rightly so in my submission, that policy and administrative changes by any government are for the most part initiated by senior public servants. If artificial language requirements prevent westerners from occupying senior or executive public service positions, the apparent misunderstanding of our problems will continue and, in fact, grow.
Let us consider what is happening. Wheat has been sold by so-called experts too cheaply and too far in advance. The world price is now over $3 a bushel but we are still filling contracts at about $1.78 a bushel. A subsidy paid in the form of acreage payments is a subsidy to consumers of bread, because we are forced by a government decision to sell wheat on the Canadian market at about $1 below the international market price. Western farmers suffer low prices at a time when the international price is high. Last year the final, realized price was the lowest in the last 10 years, namely $1.59. When the last Conservative administration made an acreage payment, it was over and above the world price of wheat.
Let us consider the feed grain problem. The western farmer does not mind the government paying feed freight assistance, but he does object to his feed grain being sold at a price 12 cents a bushel less than world prices. Western cattlemen are concerned because their representations were not listened to when the government reduced tariffs on United States cattle coming into this country, thus
Official Languages
lowering the price of their cattle by $1.50 per hundred pounds. At the same time, the government did not ask the United States to reciprocate by allowing our cattle to move just as freely into their market.

speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I am attempting to point out examples of what happens when you do not have representation in the public service from a certain area to make the views of that area known. The result is policy being formulated by a government which does not have any idea what is going on in a particular area. I suggest that if we continue to administer the bilingualism program in the way it has been administered in the past four years, these problems will continue to crop up. I am trying to point out what happens when we do not have the proper input from people who do not live in the golden triangle. That is the reason for these examples. I suggest that, politically, we in the west have endeavoured to put the point across. However, there is another part of the process, the public service, which is probably more important than the political aspect because

June 6, 1973
Official Languages
that is where policy is formulated. The result is that we end up with half-baked policies based on lack of knowledge of the area concerned.
Transportation is a very important element in the problems of Western Canada. The Prime Minister has recognized this and is willing to go to Calgary to talk about it. In 1967, it was pointed out to the government that agreed charges were bad, that captive shippers could never be proven and that public interest was difficult to prove. Having said all this, perhaps members can understand why fears and alienation will grow. Westerners have always felt that the government controlled their destiny to a greater extent than that of the people in any other part of Canada. We have seen the example of the government of Quebec opting out of very important programs. The government of Quebec appears to have arrived at a situation in which it has much more influence over the residents of that province than any other province has over its residents. Westerners have not opted out of anything. We are willing to participate but we want the opportunity to do so. This is why we are so concerned about the inability to have adequate representation at the senior level of the public service.
One could even say that this situation is the reason for the feeling that the west is continually being used by central Canada, because people from our area have a more difficult time getting to the top in Crown corporations, in the armed services and in the public service. In speaking of the armed services, I may say that we have four destroyers laid up now because the government says it cannot get people to man them. This statement is made at a time when there is supposed to be much unemployment in this country. One would think, in view of the pay scales of the armed forces, many people would be willing to take a secure and fulfilling job, but such people do not seem to be available. I wonder whether the bilingual program has anything to do with that.
Finally, in view of the Prime Minister's role in bringing about this debate at this time, I can only agree with the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) when he characterized an eating establishment in his area called "Sneaky Pete's" as being named after the Prime Minister.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few remarks before the amendment by the Leader of the Social Credit Party (Mr. Caouette) is put to the vote, because it is extremely important that all the members of this House know exactly what is its true significance.
Mr. Speaker, I am of course not questioning the intentions of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) when he put forward his motion on April 13. As I have said time and time again, it is the means to achieve the good intentions with which we do not agree, especially since we have the means not only to solve the language problem but also the constitutional problem.

This will never be repeated often enough: The problem for French-speaking Canadians is not a problem of languages but a problem of participation. Since French Canadians want at all cost to feel truly at home in this country they want to participate in the preparation of laws and in the administration and management of the country. It is simple enough.
Even if we succeeded in turning the public service into a totally bilingual body, if a fair and reasonable proportion of French-speaking people are not employed we shall have settled nothing; in fact, we shall even have accelerated the division process in this country because when Frenchspeaking Canadians will realize that they are being served in both languages but are only participating for 2, 3, or 4 per cent in the administration, they will be definitely convinced that the situation is hopeless. This is what we are trying to prevent.
In various fields this party has always been at the forefront and several years later our predictions turn out to be true. This has been happening for years, but when we are faced with the problem now before us we can no longer afford to say that this problem will be settled, that we are pioneers and that we shall settle it in 5, 10 or 20 years. Our proposal is so urgent that if we do not implement it almost immediately, I wonder where Canada is headed for.
All hon. members who have our unity at heart should most seriously consider the final settlement of this problem in Canada, to settle not a problem of language but a problem of participation.
If our objective were to enable each individual to achieve fulfilment, if it was admitted-not by paying lip service or by pious wishes-that Canada can subsist only through the active and effective participation of the francophone and anglophone communities, we would achieve something.
I am sure all my English-speaking colleagues recognize very well that Canada would not be Canada without the francophone element. Therefore it is in the interest of all my colleagues, be they from any Canadian province, to give francophones in this country the place they are entitled to. We are not asking more than that; we do not want to persecute anyone. On the contrary, we fully agree on the fact that all present public servants should keep not only the rights but the privileges they have acquired.
We agree to that. All we want is to enable now francophones to participate also on the administration level and it is by doing that that indirectly, as I said a while ago, we shall solve not only an administrative and language problem but also-and that is what is extremely important to me-a basic problem, namely that of a permanent harmony between the English and the French communities in this country.
It is in such a context that we have always examined that problem and we know objectively that it would become a secondary problem the moment the participation principle would be accepted.
That is why in paragraph 5 which is the major section of the amendment, one must see things as they are. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, is there a member in this House who could be
June 6, 1973

against such an amendment. In fact, we merely move, and I quote:
(5) that unilingualism cannot prevent a civil servant in the Canadian government from being eligible for senior positions;
Apparently then, we entirely agree with most civil servants.
I continue the quotation: therefore, the government undertakes ...
Once again, we are soft-pedalling and we would like to consider actually whether it would be possible-
... to set up, organize and implement a parallel administration, one English-speaking, the other French-speaking, in all departments of the federal government;
There would be no duplication of services nor overcrowding of the Public Service, since as explained in paragraphs (a)(b)(c) of the clause 5 of our amendment, both sections shall be proportional to the requirements of their respective administrative needs.
We entirely agree, Mr. Speaker, that in a given department in order to provide all services to our French-speaking people, we could need only 200 French-speaking employees as opposed to 1,200, 1,500 or 2,000 Englishspeaking. It could happen, depending on the services to be provided by a department.
This is then a matter of actual equality, and not of mathematical equality. This is a matter of equality according to human principles and the constitution.
Let us face it. Since we made that proposal, we have heard certain arguments from people who feared, for example, the cost of that duplication. Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the cost of such a system would probably be less than the actual cost of bilingualism, since, as it is stated in the Coulombe report, to make a public servant bilingual it costs $29,000 and to give him an insight into the other culture it costs $55,000; one knows that even if today an unilingual public servant became bilingual following those courses and the consequent expenses incurred by the government, that employee would not systematically and miraculously pass that on to others. It will be a perpetual new start and that is what we are against.
If we determine exactly what services should be provided to the French-speaking and English-speaking population of this country, and if we also determine the number of civil servants needed for each section, we are sure then of one thing: we are putting an end to the injustices that have been going on for years. And nobody would ever be dissatisfied, because those who wanted to be served in French would only have to contact the French department and those who wanted to be served in English would only have to contact the English department. Nothing could be simpler. It is like Columbus' egg. And like all simple things, it is not easy to accept. It seems too simple, because for years it has been unduly complicated, bilingualism has been overstressed at the expense of participation by the people.
Mr. Speaker, we can already foresee that if we had two departments, a French one and an English one, there would be a healthy competition that would enable all civil servants of either section to choose freely to become bilingual, not through any legal constraint but owing to the force of circumstances. This is one of the most essential
Official Languages
freedoms; it should really be left to the free will of everyone who wants to be bilingual. Everyone recognizes this need.
Mr. Speaker, some might think that I, for example, am not bilingual. Of course, I am not perfectly bilingual, but I should say that I have tried to prove that the old story I have been hearing since childhood is not quite true. As a matter of fact, I was told over and over again that to get ahead, to be successful in any field, you had to be bilingual. That was the old story I used to hear when I was young, particularly in the province of Quebec.
Well, I have attempted to show that it was possible to be a Canadian while speaking French. Unfortunately today I have to bear the consequences of the principle I have tried to demonstrate and I am really anxious to be bilingual myself. But, Mr. Speaker, it is in that context that we see the problem. As I have said before, we are not motivated by emotion or spite but we are sure that we can offer a concrete solution which could at least be considered and furthermore which could really save Canada if we were to set up a system by which all French-speaking people in this country could participate in the management of the nation. That would depend only on their qualifications and therefore, there would not be anymore injustice. Is that not all what we want?
There already has been references to the "just society". It has been said already that we want for this country understanding, unity, and harmony. But why? To do that, Mr. Speaker, why do we not take the required steps? Why these further attempts with good intentions? Why are we frustrating the French-speaking Canadians by telling them that it is very difficult to change the civil service because it has been in existence for so many years-that is why people refer to it as an English-speaking establishment-and we must proceed slowly. They tried to implement certain changes after having passed the Official Language Act, but they realized that politically it was not good, and then they said: Let us back up a little bit, let us please the civil servants and then afterwards we shall see!
Mr. Speaker, once more, we do not take a pessimistic approach to the right hon. Prime Minister's intentions and these nine principles, these nine steps he wants to take to achieve his goal; it is not a matter of being pessimistic but we want to stop thinking in terms of wishes, pious hopes and even miracles. As a matter of fact, I read that if someone wants to obtain a bilingual position, he simply has to indicate his willingness to become bilingual.
We do not believe very easily in this gift of tongues. We do know that although this has already happened in the Cenacle for the Apostles, but we do not believe that to-day, a public servant may become bilingual just because he wishes to. That is too much!
That is the reason why, without trying to interfere with anybody's rights and privileges, we could do justice to French-speaking Canadians, and to English-speaking Canadians everywhere in this country, by merely adopting our amendment.
Mr. Speaker, when we mentioned this part of our political platform to our own party-I remember quite well, having presented it myself-our delegates from British

June 6, 1973
Official Languages
Columbia, Alberta and Manitoba told me: We are not only in agreement with this proposition, we are behind it 200%, which means that we may be the only political party with sympathizers in all parts of Canada and, whether in British Columbia, Newfoundland or Quebec, our message is always the same, thereby assuring all Canadians of the prospect of self-reliance and self-development, while maintaining their true identity.
Therefore, this is not a last minute amendment that we are proposing now but an amendment which has been thought out and which has already been proposed to our delegates from every part of this country who have adopted it right away. This is why, Mr. Speaker, we should like the government and all the hon. members to merely support it. Then they could rightfully claim the glory and honour of having not only settled the constitutional problem, but also the problem of Canada as a whole.
